dose_basis_enum.definition: Ingredient amount charged into one documented formula/manufacturing batch.

Ingredient amount attributable to one finished unit only when the source directly states it or it can be calculated from explicit ingredient batch input plus explicit finished-unit yield/count with no missing process factor.
dose_basis_enum.warning: Use 'nominal apportioned input' when calculated from batch/yield; do not call it measured systemic exposure.

dose_basis_enum.definition: Adult usual daily amount in a single-herb/decoction-piece monograph; ChP 2025 general principles support this interpretation unless otherwise specified.
Amount exactly as printed in the historical source, preserving original unit/wording; no silent gram conversion.
Finished-product mass expressed as equivalent to a stated mass of decoction pieces/crude drug, e.g. '每1g相当于饮片0.98g'.

recommended_model.critical_rule: `malformed` is not a dose basis. It is a quality/status flag. Keep semantics and data-quality state orthogonal.

why: Historical medical metrology changed over time.
Even Eastern Han/Zhang Zhongjing conversion has published competing estimates (15 g/liang vs 13.8 g/liang).
Song-period medical units and later market units cannot be treated as one universal coefficient.
A modern secondary source may already embed a conversion; that converted value is source-provided normalization, not the original text.

allowed_conversion_cases.rule: Conversion may be stored with source-specific coefficient and provenance.
Store original amount and official converted amount separately; do not reverse-engineer a universal dynasty coefficient.
May use 1 liang = 31.25 g and 1 qian = 3.125 g, citing A3S18. Never apply this coefficient to Han/Song classical text merely because the characters 两/钱 match.

disallowed_cases: Automatically converting all Han/Tang/Song/Ming/Qing prescriptions with one qian/liang coefficient.
Inferring a dynasty from formula name alone.
Using a textbook's parenthetical gram value as proof that the historical original itself was written in grams.
Converting count/size units such as 枚, 梧桐子大 without a source-specific weight study.

evidence_examples.claim: Explicit old market 16-liang system: 1 liang = 31.25 g; 1 qian = 3.125 g.

required_inputs: ingredient batch input amount with matching formulation version
explicit final finished-unit count or validated final product yield
no unaccounted extraction, discard, concentration, coating, excipient or processing factor that makes simple proportional allocation invalid

formula_examples.why: Zhu Sha 100 g and exactly 960 finished pills are stated in the same formula standard.
formula_examples.result: 100/960 g ≈ 0.10417 g = 104.17 mg nominal Zhu Sha input per pill; not a measured pharmacokinetic exposure.

formula_examples.why: 3 g finished pill and daily unit dose are known, but batch output count/validated yield is not supplied in the cited source.
Xi Xin 18 g batch input is known, but explicit final batch unit count is not supplied; honey ratio is not a final yield.
Prepared aconites 180 g each and honey addition ratio are known, but final unit count/yield is not explicit. Do not derive aconite per 3 g pill.
